dek: Six Great Smoky Mountains waterfalls in North Carolina and Tennessee. No entrance fee, but you need a parking tag. Laurel Falls is the shortest published walk.
overview: Great Smoky Mountains National Park straddles the North Carolina and Tennessee line and calls itself the most visited national park in the country. The park says its high country averages more than 85 inches of rain a year and the lowlands about 55, so there isn't one snowmelt season to plan around.

We cover six waterfalls: Mouse Creek Falls on the North Carolina side, and Abrams Falls, Grotto Falls, Laurel Falls, Ramsey Cascades and Hen Wallow Falls in Tennessee. The park calls Ramsey Cascades the tallest waterfall in the Smokies, and lists Abrams, Grotto, Laurel and Rainbow Falls as the hikes that together see more than 200,000 visits a year. (Rainbow Falls isn't covered here.)
fallsIntro: Ramsey Cascades is the big hike, and Laurel Falls is the shorter, busier one. Ramsey's distance and climb come from the park's waterfall page; Laurel's comes from our trail file.
plan: Laurel Falls is the short hike at 1.2 miles one way. The park lists it among the crowded ones and says parking is often limited. A parking tag is required if you stop for more than 15 minutes, and most trailheads don't sell tags, so buy one before you reach the lot.

Ramsey Cascades is the long hike: an 8-mile round trip with more than 2,100 feet of climbing, which the park calls challenging. Save it for a separate day if you want the tallest waterfall rather than the busiest one. We don't have walk lengths for Abrams Falls, Grotto Falls, Hen Wallow Falls or Mouse Creek Falls.
feesLead: There is no entrance fee, but you need a parking tag if you stop anywhere in the park for more than 15 minutes. America the Beautiful passes don't replace it.
access: Tags cost $5 for a day, $15 for a week or $40 for a year. They must be the physical tag displayed in your vehicle (a screenshot doesn't count), and a tag doesn't reserve a parking space. Many trailheads have no machine, so buy one in advance.
safety: The park says water recreation is not recommended. Drowning is one of the leading causes of death in the park, and its waterfall page ties injuries to swimming, climbing around waterfalls and tubing. Stay on the trail and out of the water.
